stem.en: A drug stops splicing in a human cell. Kabir says "bacteria would be hit even harder, since they are simpler". What happens to each?

text.en: The human cell stops making most of its proteins, since most human genes have introns. The bacterium is untouched: it has no introns and no splicing, so there is nothing to stop.

feedback.en: Bacterial genes are written straight through. A splicing inhibitor finds nothing to inhibit.

text.en: The bacterium dies and the human cell is fine.

feedback.en: Backwards. The human cell depends on splicing; the bacterium never needed it.

text.en: Neither is affected, because splicing is optional.

feedback.en: An intron left in makes a truncated, useless protein, from VI.5 L02. For a human cell, splicing is not optional.

explanation.en: Ask whether the target exists in each cell. Splicing exists in eukaryotes and not in bacteria. The drug's effect follows.
